question: A product manager asks an engineer to justify why the team began prototyping a new feature with Claude Haiku 4.5 instead of Claude Opus 4.8, even though Opus 4.8 has higher raw capability. Which of the following are valid justifications drawn from Anthropic's guidance on starting with a fast, cost-effective model? (Select all that apply)
options: A) Claude Haiku 4.5 must be used first because Claude Opus 4.8 cannot be accessed until a Haiku-based prototype has been benchmarked
B) The approach is well suited to applications with tight latency requirements
C) Starting with a faster, more cost-effective model allows for quick iteration during initial prototyping and development
D) The approach is well suited to cost-sensitive implementations and high-volume, straightforward tasks
E) Starting with Haiku 4.5 guarantees the same accuracy as Opus 4.8 on every task, making the choice of starting model irrelevant to quality
correct_answers: B) The approach is well suited to applications with tight latency requirements
C) Starting with a faster, more cost-effective model allows for quick iteration during initial prototyping and development
D) The approach is well suited to cost-sensitive implementations and high-volume, straightforward tasks
explanations: Incorrect. There is no such access restriction; teams may start directly with Opus 4.8 under the alternative 'start with the most capable model' approach for complex reasoning tasks, with no requirement to benchmark on Haiku first.
Correct. Applications with tight latency requirements are explicitly listed as a best fit for starting with a fast, cost-effective model like Haiku 4.5.

Correct. The documentation states this approach allows for quick iteration, lower development costs, and is often sufficient for many common applications, explicitly listing initial prototyping and development as a best fit.
Correct. Cost-sensitive implementations and high-volume, straightforward tasks are explicitly listed as best fits for this starting approach.

Incorrect. The guidance explicitly frames upgrading as necessary when performance does not meet requirements, meaning accuracy is not guaranteed to be equivalent; the recommendation is to test thoroughly and upgrade only if there are specific capability gaps.
